thread.title: More Bad News for Apple Stock: Signs Its Services Growth Could Slow

title: More Bad News for Apple Stock: Signs Its Services Growth Could Slow
text:
Apple Stock Could Suffer From Slowing Growth for Services Business By Dec. 12, 2018 2:22 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Greg Baker/AFP/Getty Images Text size
Even as Apple stock has plunged in recent weeks on concerns about deteriorating iPhone sales, some Wall Street analysts have taken solace in their long-term optimism on its services business.
But now Macquarie Research analyst Benjamin Schachter is getting less bullish about the outlook for Apple services, too, predicting the segment will see a slowing growth rate next year. While Schachter reiterated his Outperform rating on the stock, he lowered his price target for Apple shares to $188 from $222.
Apple (ticker: AAPL) stock was up 1.6% to $171.24 on Wednesday.
“Unfortunately, right as investors are becoming more interested in Services as a meaningful part of the story, we think it is now about to slow,” he wrote Wednesday.
Licensing, the App Store and Apple Care are the main drivers likely to drag on the segment, Schachter said, adding that the company’s faster growing businesses—Apple Music, iCloud and Apple Pay—are “not big enough to offset.”
The analyst said the Asia Pacific region accounted for nearly 60% of App Store spending last year and was a key driver of the business for the last two years. But that, too, could change.
“The strength of APAC has been a tailwind, but we think that could turn in 2019, led by first and foremost the freeze of new game registration in China that will start to become a more prominent drag on new game spending into next year,” Schachter wrote.
Chinese regulators haven’t approved the sale of new video game titles since March amid concerns some games were too addictive or violent.
Apple’s shares have declined more than 20% since the end of October as concerns have mounted about weak demand for the newest iPhone models. Newsletter Sign-up
Last month, The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Apple cut orders for all three newly released iPhone models.
If the concerns over slowing iPhone demand prove accurate, Schachter also expects lower sales for its Apple Care business, which relies on hardware revenue.
As a result, he estimates the sales growth rate for the services segment will fall to 22% in fiscal 2019 from 26% in fiscal 2018.
